## Not duplicates

lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-relative-canonical-root-exponential: the existing node assumes a Noetherian base and states the single-root exponential; the new statement works over every nonzero ring and also supplies linked negative generators, Weyl representatives and their relations, closed root-set products, open-cell generation and self-centralizing tori. It is not a one-line specialization of the existing node.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-relative-opposite-root-reflection-map: that statement assumes a Noetherian ring and supplies a single-root reflection map, not arbitrary-ring closed root-set products or the full pinned relation data.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-local-split-root-data-weyl-lifts: the existing statement is restricted to Noetherian local bases and gives choices of Weyl lifts, not the pinned square and cubic relations or closed root-set products over arbitrary rings.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-relative-root-product-open-cell: the existing node assumes a Noetherian local base and treats the positive and negative full systems; it does not state the arbitrary-ring calculus, closed subsets, or Weyl relations.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-split-reductive-local-gauss-atlas: the existing node gives a coordinate atlas over a Noetherian local ring, not pinned root-group relations over arbitrary rings.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-split-positive-root-borel: the existing node states existence and uniqueness of the positive-root Borel; it gives no root-group products, Weyl representatives, their relations, or generation statement.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations: the existing statement is over an algebraically closed field, and contains no general-ring Weyl-relation or root-product theorem.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-opposite-root-sl2-parametrizations: the existing statement constructs a rank-one SL2 map over an algebraically closed field; it does not provide the arbitrary-ring root-set products and pinned Weyl calculus.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-relative-root-rank-one-centralizer: the existing node identifies a rank-one centralizer, not root-group products and Weyl representatives.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-quasifinite-root-map-rigidity: that theorem assumes an already existing quasi-finite surjective homomorphism between two reductive groups; here there is no such map, and the conclusion is internal group geometry.
lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus vs lem-sfb-standard-parabolic-levi-charts: the existing field-only parabolic theorem does not cover arbitrary coefficient rings or state the pinned Weyl relations.
lem-sfb-pinned-root-relations-hom-criterion vs lem-sfb-small-centralizer-hom-amalgamation: the new node takes torus maps, simple-root maps, sections and explicit algebraic relations, with no supplied maps from whole reductive centralizers; the item must construct those data and prove all relations. The new statement is Conrad Theorem 6.2.4, not Corollary 6.2.7 and not a clause of the item.
lem-sfb-pinned-root-relations-hom-criterion vs lem-sfb-low-rank-pinned-root-hom: the latter constructs special isogenies between pinned reductive groups of rank at most two; the criterion accepts arbitrary affine target groups and arbitrary semisimple rank, using relation data rather than a root-datum isogeny.
lem-sfb-pinned-root-relations-hom-criterion vs lem-sfb-quasifinite-root-map-rigidity: the existing statement is rigidity of quasi-finite surjective maps between reductive groups; the new one constructs an arbitrary-target homomorphism from explicit relations and has no quasi-finite or surjectivity assumption.

## Review by Q132

I read delivery-errors.md B--E in full, including the repeated archived copy. I checked that each new node introduces its base, group schemes and data, cites the existing definition of a pinned realization, has no proof or proof dependencies, and is an independently usable prerequisite rather than a restated clause. I read the statements of all cited nodes. I compared the new geometry statement with Conrad Theorem 4.1.4 (canonical equivariant exponential), Corollary 5.1.9 and Remark 5.1.10 (linked generators, reflection, square and cubic identities), Proposition 5.1.6 and Corollary 5.1.11 (Weyl quotient), Theorem 5.1.13 and Proposition 5.1.16 (open cell and closed root-set products), and the opening of Section 6.2 (multiplication of two open cells). Self-centralizing maximal tori are Proposition 3.1.9(2); semisimple rank is the rank of the root system. The reductive-subgroup compatibility follows by applying the uniquely characterized root exponential and the rank-one coroot construction to the subgroup containing the same torus. I compared every hypothesis and displayed identity of the relation criterion to Theorem 6.2.4 and its uniqueness preamble, not just to the final corollary.

Step 1 uses the finite-basis theorem exactly for the finitely generated torsion-free quotient. I wrote out saturation, the surviving monomial test, and the support-in-J argument. The diagonalizable duality node explicitly states the closed-immersion criterion for a surjective character map. This supplies an embedded split torus, not a possibly nonsmooth diagonalizable kernel.

Step 2 uses the relative centralizer-normalizer node for smooth represented centralizers and invariant Lie modules. Its hypotheses hold because G is smooth affine of finite presentation and S_J is a closed split torus. The automorphism-fixed-group node explicitly preserves reductivity under a torus action; conjugation is such an action and its fixed functor is the required centralizer. The bundle-weights node explicitly identifies the invariant direct sum for a free quotient lattice, with arbitrary base change. I checked that it has no Noetherian assumption. The definition of the realization supplies precisely the global weight decomposition and geometric maximality used here. Thus the argument applies to nonreduced and disconnected A, not just to field fibres.

Step 3 uses the new geometry statement for inherited root exponentials/coroots, root rank, self-centralizing T and root-group generation. The subgroup is already reductive and contains the same maximal torus, so these hypotheses are available before applying compatibility. The inclusion for I subset J is reversed at the level of subtori and then reversed again for centralizers; I checked the direction explicitly. For J=Delta, the subtorus need not be trivial when G has a central torus: instead all root characters vanish on it and generation proves it central. For J empty, self-centralizing T gives G_empty=T. If Delta is empty these two equalities coincide and the given torus map is the unique extension.

Step 4 uses the new geometry statement to put each root group and Weyl representative inside the appropriate centralizer and to form the two-root positive subgroup. Its root set includes alpha and beta (the coefficients are nonnegative, not both strictly positive). The compatibility hypotheses on g_J identify its restrictions with the chosen simple-root maps and identify all torus restrictions with g_empty.

Step 5 uses the identities in the geometry statement, then applies actual given homomorphisms to them. I checked both torus-conjugation identities, the square, the cubic, the rank-two Weyl relation, and both root-conjugation identities individually against the new criterion. In the last identities s_alpha(c) stays positive for c different from alpha because its beta coefficient remains positive, so the right side really lies in the domain of q_alpha_beta. The values on n_alpha agree across the two-root subgroup by the original compatibility assumption, not by an assertion about tangent vectors.

Step 6 uses exactly the existence and uniqueness conclusions of the criterion. The affine target H meets its target hypothesis without a smoothness, reducedness or finite-presentation assumption. After construction I checked restrictions to G_J using that criterion's separate uniqueness clause for the inherited base J. This avoids the unsupported inference that agreeing on the two given positive root groups already gives a prescribed whole subgroup map. Global uniqueness is the same criterion for G. All citations have verbatim quotes in citations.json.

Small cases checked: the torus case; simple rank one (the supplied singleton is already G); rank two (the supplied pair is G); product root systems including the orthogonal-pair m=2 case; a central torus factor where S_Delta is nontrivial; characteristic 2 where alpha^vee(-1) can be the identity but the square and cubic identities still hold; and rings with nilpotents or idempotent decompositions. The root-subgroup statements used here are group-scheme assertions after every algebra extension; abstract point-group amalgamation would not suffice. None of the six proof steps exceeds 2000 characters. I corrected the preliminary plan by deleting the proposed new smooth-centralizer node and citing the already-existing arbitrary-base results instead. No statement dispute was needed.
